title: Sines, cosines, and cross projections
subtitle: G2 lecture 043000 · expanded companion
adaptation: Individually authored from the spoken lecture and its display-only mathematical appendix. Includes stepwise constructions, explicit hypotheses, worked examples and topic-specific vector figures; all slide prose is independent of audio.

slides.title: Two pieces of the same frame
slides.lead: Given a trial frame E and target projection Q, split every trial vector into its kept and rejected components.
body: Assume E*E=I. The overlap map C=QE lands inside the target subspace, while the escape map S=(I−Q)E lands in its orthogonal complement.
The two outputs are orthogonal for every input. Their Gram operators therefore add to the identity on the frame coordinate space.
slides.takeaway: Overlap and escape are orthogonal pieces of one isometric frame.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 043000 · Two pieces of the same frame

slides.title: The Pythagorean operator calculation
slides.lead: The algebra is a one-line use of Q²=Q and E*E=I.
body: Compute C*C=E*QE and S*S=E*(I−Q)E. Adding gives E*(Q+I−Q)E=E*E=I.
This identity is stronger than a picture: it holds simultaneously for every frame-coordinate vector, so the squared cosine and sine operators complement each other.
slides.takeaway: The cosine-squared and sine-squared operators add exactly to identity.

slides.title: One tilted direction
slides.lead: Let E send the scalar 1 to a unit vector e in U, and let V be a line at angle θ.
body: The target projection keeps a component of length cos θ along V. Its perpendicular remainder has length sin θ. Because the components are orthogonal, their squared lengths sum to one.
At θ=0 the escape vanishes; at θ=π/2 the overlap vanishes. Intermediate angles interpolate continuously between these endpoints.
slides.takeaway: A single directed sine is the magnitude of the perpendicular escape.

slides.title: From one angle to many
slides.lead: The singular values of C encode cosine overlap, while those of S encode directed sine escape.
body: Because C*C and S*S=I−C*C commute and share eigenvectors, their eigenvalues pair as cos²θ_i and sin²θ_i.
The resulting operators are basis-independent descriptions of the angles from U toward V. Their singular values give simultaneous quantitative control on multiple directions.
slides.takeaway: Sine and cosine share principal directions even when there are many of them.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 043000 · From one angle to many

slides.title: When dimensions differ, direction matters
slides.lead: Escape from U to V need not equal escape from V to U.
body: If U is a plane and V a line contained in it, one direction of U lies inside V while another is orthogonal to V. Thus the U-to-V escape map has norm one.
But every vector in V already belongs to U, so the V-to-U escape map vanishes. A theorem about rectangular angles must specify its source and target subspaces.
slides.takeaway: Directed sine is sensitive to unmatched dimensions.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 043000 · When dimensions differ, direction matters

slides.title: Compare the two ambient projections
slides.lead: The difference P−Q acts on every ambient vector, not only on vectors from U.
body: Its square splits into a P-side escape and a complementary Q-side escape. These two terms act on orthogonal P and I−P blocks, allowing their norms to be compared.
The operator-norm distance between projections is the larger of the two directed escape norms.
slides.takeaway: Projection distance captures the worst escape in either direction.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 043000 · Compare the two ambient projections

slides.title: Why the square splits cleanly
slides.lead: Expand the two sides using idempotence of P and Q.
body: On the left, (P−Q)²=P+Q−PQ−QP. On the right, P(I−Q)P+(I−P)Q(I−P) expands to exactly the same expression.
The first summand acts on ran P, the second on ran(I−P); as positive blocks they cannot interfere. This is the algebra behind the max formula.
slides.takeaway: The squared projection difference separates the two directions of escape.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 043000 · Why the square splits cleanly

slides.title: A forty-five-degree check
slides.lead: Take U horizontal and V tilted at θ=π/4 in the plane.
body: Both directions have escape norm sin(π/4)=1/√2, so ||P−Q||=1/√2. The squared difference has norm 1/2.
This elementary case checks that the formula measures angles rather than just comparing the coordinate entries of P and Q.
slides.takeaway: Projection distance recovers the sine of the principal angle for two lines.

slides.title: An unequal-dimension matrix check
slides.lead: The directed escape asymmetry appears even for diagonal projection matrices.
body: In R³ take U=span(e₁,e₂) and V=span(e₁). Then P=diag(1,1,0), while Q=diag(1,0,0). Applying I−Q to P retains the e₂ direction, so its operator norm is one.
By contrast, (I−P)Q=0 because every vector of V is already in U. The difference P−Q=diag(0,1,0) has norm one, matching the max formula exactly.
slides.takeaway: The two directional errors can differ, and projection distance takes the larger one.

slides.title: Rebuild the chain of identities
slides.lead: Start with one isometric frame and one orthogonal projection.
body: Prove C*C+S*S=I, diagonalize C*C, and interpret its eigenvalues as cosine-squared principal angles. Next expand (P−Q)² to obtain the max-of-escapes formula.
Check the unequal-dimensional plane-line example to see why the direction labels cannot be omitted in general.
slides.takeaway: Sine maps, cosine maps, and projection differences are related but distinct measurements.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 043000 · Rebuild the chain of identities
